Game theory is just a study of how to win games. It's a very general thing. Let's say there's about a million people in the world, all trying to win against each other, but only one can win. According to game theory, the best way to win a game is by cheating. If you follow the rules, you will never win; you have to cheat. And in this game, the best way to win is by coordinating with others, right? Because everyone's playing alone. So if you can work with other people, that gives you a huge advantage over everyone else.

The problem with this coordination is it forces an arms race of cooperation. Maybe these two are working together; now these four have to work together, which forces these five to join. If you are the first to coordinate, you get screwed in the process. So if you cheat, you have to cheat. You have to coordinate without people knowing you're actually coordinating together; you have to conspire secretly.

Family is one example of coordination, synchronicity. Another example is religion. If you have a leader, similar race or ethnicity, and a shared language, these are examples of how you get people to coordinate. The problem is that these strategies are obvious, forcing everyone else to do the same thing. But there's a strategy that allows you to coordinate secretly and defeat all your enemies. This strategy is called transgression.

Transgression means breaking taboos, social norms, or laws. The idea is that the greater the level of transgression, the greater your cohesion which leads to synchronicity. Transgression forces cohesion because anyone who betrays the secret risks being punished by everyone else in the group. We see this in all aspects of society; for example, a joke among six friends—covering rooms with toilet paper makes you more cohesive because keeping it a secret strengthens the bond.

When you transgress, everyone wants to punish you, which means that the only way to survive is by keeping the secret within your group, forcing cohesion.
